Bayesian evidence & model selection

Physics × Machine Learning — Bayesian inference

How many things are in the data?
Model selection by the evidence

The best fit always improves as you add parameters — more knobs can only fit better. The Bayesian evidence does not: it peaks at the right level of complexity and then falls. That is Occam’s razor made quantitative — and the same calculation decides “how many planets?”, “does the universe need dark-energy evolution?”, and “is there a signal here at all?”

The tension

Maximum likelihood can never tell you when to stop adding components — a bigger model always fits at least as well. Chasing fit alone guarantees over-fitting.

The resolution

The evidence rewards fit but charges for flexibility. It automatically prefers the simplest model that explains the data — no hand-tuned threshold.

Two worked examples

Counting Gaussian bumps, and choosing a polynomial degree. In both, the evidence lands on the truth.

How to compute it

Closed form for linear models, the Laplace / Occam-factor approximation, BIC, nested sampling, and modern neural estimators.

Real science

Worked cases from cosmology, inflation, exoplanets and gravitational waves — where the evidence is the deciding number.

The evidence, and why it embodies Occam’s razor

Compare two models, each with a prior π(θ) over its parameters and a likelihood L(θ). The evidence is the probability the model assigns to the data before seeing it, averaged over every setting the prior allows:

Z  =  p(data | model)  =  ∫ L(θ)   π(θ)   dθ the marginal likelihood: the likelihood averaged over the whole prior

Model comparison is then a ratio of evidences — the Bayes factor B = Z1 / Z0 — times the ratio of prior beliefs. No reference to a best-fit point; the whole prior is integrated. The Bayes factor is read on the empirical Jeffreys scale: |ln B| above ~1 is ‘substantial’, above ~2.5 ‘strong’, above ~5 ‘decisive’ evidence for one model over the other.

Why complex models are penalised

A flexible model spreads its prior mass over a huge parameter space, most of which the data rule out. That dilution is the penalty. Expand the integral around the best fit θ* and you get the Occam factor:

Z  ≈  L(θ*)  ×  ( Δθposterior ⁄ Δθprior ) best-fit likelihood × the fraction of prior space the data leave plausible

The first factor is how well the model fits; the second, always ≤ 1, is how much of its prior range the data collapsed. An extra parameter multiplies in another factor < 1. So a component that barely improves the fit lowers the evidence — the razor, quantified. Notice the prior matters: the evidence genuinely depends on how wide a net the model casts, which is a feature, not a bug.

Example 1: how many bumps are in the signal?

The data are a sum of an unknown number of fixed-width Gaussian bumps plus noise. For each model — M = 1, 2, 3, 4 assumed bumps — we compute the evidence ZM, marginalising the linear amplitudes analytically and integrating the bump positions on a grid (dividing by M! for the components’ interchangeability). The truth is two bumps.

Left: data with the best M = 1, 2, 3 fits. Right: best-fit log-likelihood (grey) vs log-evidence (blue); the inset zooms into M = 2, 3, 4.

The best fit (grey) climbs from M = 1 to M = 2 and then keeps creeping up — extra bumps always find a little more noise to absorb. The evidence (blue) jumps by over 100 in log units to M = 2, then falls (−9.1 → −14.2 → −15.3). It peaks precisely at the true count.

Read-off. Selecting the model at the evidence peak recovers the right number of sources. Maximum likelihood alone never would. This is exactly the “how many planets / how many blended sources” question, in miniature.

Example 2: what degree of polynomial?

A different model, the same lesson — and here the evidence is exact, no grid. The data come from a cubic plus noise; we fit polynomials of degree D = 0…8. Because a polynomial is linear in its coefficients, with a Gaussian prior on them the whole evidence integral is a single Gaussian and has a closed form (see “How to calculate (I)”).

Left: data with degree 1, 3, 8 fits — degree 8 already wiggles at the edges (over-fitting). Right: fit keeps improving with D while the evidence peaks sharply at the true degree 3.

Maximum log-likelihood rises monotonically (−16.7 at D = 3 to −15.1 at D = 8) — every extra term helps the fit a little. The evidence peaks exactly at D = 3 (−31.7) and then declines steadily: each needless coefficient pays an Occam factor and buys almost nothing.

Interactive: drag the degree and watch Occam’s razor

Drag the slider to change the polynomial degree D. The left panel shows the fit; the right panel tracks the max-likelihood (grey, always improving) against the log-evidence (blue, peaking at the truth). Push D high and the fit wiggles to chase noise — the evidence sees straight through it.

Left: the real data (grey) with the degree-D least-squares fit (blue) and the true cubic (dashed). Right: relative log-evidence (blue squares) and max-likelihood (grey circles); the red star marks the current D.
Why this example matters. It is the cleanest “how to calculate” case: the evidence has a formula you can evaluate directly. That same closed form is the engine inside the bump example, inside radial-velocity planet searches, and inside satellite-RFI amplitude marginalisation.

Computing the evidence, part I: when you can do it (nearly) exactly

1. Linear–Gaussian models — closed form

If the model is linear in its parameters, d = Φw + noise with Gaussian noise (variance σ²) and a Gaussian prior w ∼ N(0, A), then d is itself Gaussian and the evidence integral is done in one line:

Z  =  N( d  |  0,   C ),    C  =  σ²I  +  Φ A ΦT log Z = −½ [ dTC−1d  +  log |2πC| ]

This is exactly what Example 2 evaluates (Φ = the polynomial design matrix), and — via the matrix-determinant lemma / Woodbury identity — what marginalises the source amplitudes in Example 1 and in satellite-RFI work. Whenever some parameters enter linearly, integrate those out in closed form and only sample the rest. That is the VARPRO trick, and it is what makes these calculations fast.

2. The Laplace approximation — a Gaussian around the peak

For a smooth posterior that is roughly Gaussian near its maximum θ*, expand to second order. With H the Hessian of −log(Lπ) at the peak:

Z  ≈  L(θ*)   π(θ*)   (2π)k/2   |H|−1/2 fit at the peak × the posterior volume (k = number of parameters)

This is the Occam factor of page 2 written out: |H|−1/2 is the posterior width. It needs only the best fit and the curvature there — cheap, and often good enough to rank models.

3. BIC — the large-data shortcut

Take the Laplace result to the limit of many data points n and only the leading terms survive:

−2 log Z  ≈  −2 log Lmax  +  k &log; n  ≡  BIC fit term + a penalty of (½ log n) per parameter

No integral, no Hessian — just the best-fit likelihood and a parameter count. A quick first pass; the exact or Laplace value is what you trust when models are close. (Its cousin the AIC penalises differently and answers a subtly different question — predictive accuracy rather than truth.)

Computing the evidence, part II: the general, nonlinear case

When the posterior is multimodal or far from Gaussian, approximations fail and you integrate numerically. These are the workhorses.

Nested sampling

Reparametrise by the prior volume X enclosed above a likelihood level, turning the multi-dimensional integral into a 1-D one:

Z = ∫01 L(X) dX

A set of “live points” is evolved, the worst replaced by a better one each step, sweeping from prior to peak. Gives Z and posterior samples together. Tools: MultiNest, PolyChord, dynesty, UltraNest — the standard in cosmology and RFI work.

Thermodynamic integration & bridge sampling

Introduce a temperature β that morphs prior into posterior and integrate the average log-likelihood along it:

log Z = ∫01 ⟨ log L ⟩β dβ

Robust for tough, multimodal posteriors; needs several MCMC chains at different β. Bridge / stepping-stone sampling are related estimators that reuse MCMC output.

Savage–Dickey ratio — for detection

When one model is the other with a parameter fixed (e.g. amplitude θ = 0 ⇄ “no source”), the Bayes factor is just a ratio of densities at that point:

B10 = π(θ=0) ⁄ p(θ=0 | data)

Prior over posterior at the null value — readable straight off the posterior you already sampled. Exactly the “is there a signal?” test.

Neural & ML estimators (new)

Recent work learns the evidence or the Bayes factor directly: the learnt harmonic mean (a machine-learned target that fixes the classic estimator’s instability), normalizing-flow nested sampling (nessai), and amortized classifiers such as Evidence Networks that output a Bayes factor in one forward pass — the frontier for simulation-based inference. See the references page.

Rule of thumb. Linear parameters → marginalise in closed form. Smooth & unimodal → Laplace / BIC to rank quickly. Nasty & multimodal → nested sampling for Z and the posterior at once. Expensive simulator, many comparisons → a neural estimator.

Model selection in the wild

The same evidence calculation decides open questions across astrophysics. In every case the pattern is the one from the two demos: a bigger model fits at least as well, and the evidence adjudicates whether the extra structure is warranted.

Is the standard cosmological model complete?

ΛCDM has just six parameters. Does the data demand more — spatial curvature Ωk, an evolving dark-energy equation of state w(z), extra relativistic species Neff, a running spectral index? Bayesian evidence has repeatedly favoured plain ΛCDM over these extensions (Heavens et al. 2017): the extra parameters pay an Occam penalty they do not yet earn.

Which model of inflation?

Hundreds of inflaton potentials have been proposed. Using the Planck data, Bayesian evidence ranks them (Martin, Ringeval & Trotta 2014): simple plateau potentials win, and large classes are decisively disfavoured — model selection over a whole zoo of theories at once.

Cosmological tensions: new physics or systematics?

Is the Hubble tension a real crack in the model? Evidence-ratio and suspiciousness statistics (Handley & Lemos 2019) recast “how many σ” as a prior-independent model comparison between “one consistent universe” and “two datasets, two truths.”

How many planets?

Each planet adds ~5 nonlinear parameters to a radial-velocity curve. The evidence chooses between an N- and (N+1)-planet model (Gregory 2007; Feroz, Balan & Hobson 2011) — the sky version of Example 1, and a textbook use of nested sampling.

Gravitational waves

LIGO/Virgo report a detection Bayes factor (signal vs noise), compare source hypotheses, and test whether the data need deviations from General Relativity — all Bayesian model selection, run in pipelines such as Bilby.

Source detection & deblending

How many sources sit in a crowded field or a single beam, and is a candidate real or noise? The same M-vs-(M+1) evidence comparison — and precisely the structure of the satellite-RFI problem: detection is 0-vs-1 source, deblending is larger M, with the amplitudes marginalised in closed form.

Common thread. “Do we need this extra parameter / component / source?” is one question with one answer: compare the evidences. The razor does the deciding.

Worked calculation I: dark energy from real supernovae

Not a cartoon — this is the actual Bayesian calculation on real data: 40 binned Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon compilation (redshifts z = 0.01–1.6). Each SN gives an apparent magnitude; the unknown absolute-magnitude/H0 offset is a single linear parameter, marginalised analytically. We then compute the evidence for three cosmologies, integrating over the matter density Ωm (and w) with flat priors.

Left: the real SN Ia Hubble diagram, with best-fit ΛCDM and a decelerating Einstein–de Sitter universe; the inset shows residuals. Right: the Bayesian evidence — EdS is decisively excluded, while ΛCDM and w​CDM are tied.

The result reproduces two landmark conclusions. First, the data decisively demand acceleration: ln B(ΛCDM : Einstein–de Sitter) ≈ 700 — off any scale, the 1998 dark-energy discovery in one number. The best-fit matter density comes out Ωm ≈ 0.28, right where it should. Second, does the data need dark energy beyond a cosmological constant? Allowing a free equation of state w gives |ln B(ΛCDM : w​CDM)| < 1 — inconclusive. The extra parameter is not earned; Occam keeps the simpler Λ.

Methodology on display. Analytic marginalisation of the linear offset + grid integration of the nonlinear cosmological parameters — exactly the recipe from “How to calculate (I)”, applied to real supernovae.

Worked calculation II: counting planets, and detecting a signal

Two more genuine calculations, run with the same machinery. Left problem: how many planets in a radial-velocity curve? Each planet is a Keplerian wobble — amplitudes linear (marginalised analytically), periods nonlinear (integrated on a log grid). Right problem: is there a signal in the noise at all?

Mock two-planet RV data. The evidence climbs to M = 2 and then falls (a spurious third planet is penalised); the inset periodogram finds both true periods (12 & 43 d). ln B(2:1) = +111, ln B(3:2) = −28.

The evidence peaks at the true count of two planets and recovers their periods (12.3, 42.9 d) with no input other than the data — the Gregory (2007) / Feroz–Balan–Hobson (2011) method in miniature. A third planet lowers the evidence: the razor again.

Detection = model selection between “noise only” (M = 0) and “one source” (M = 1). As the injected signal-to-noise rises, the Bayes factor climbs out of the inconclusive band and past the decisive threshold — a principled detection statistic.

This last panel is the “is there a signal at all?” test that underlies gravitational-wave detection, astronomical source-finding, and the satellite-RFI problem: a faint pulse is recovered and scored by its Bayes factor, with the threshold set by the evidence rather than an arbitrary cut.

Interactive: detect a signal, and the 5σ gold standard

Drag the signal-to-noise slider (or press Collect data) and watch a faint pulse emerge from noise and its log Bayes factor climb out of the inconclusive band, past ‘decisive’, toward discovery. The same statistic drives particle physics: the Higgs boson was claimed only once the excess reached 5σ — a Bayes factor and a p-value are two views of the one question, “is this real?”

Dark: noisy data. Blue: the recovered pulse (amplitude marginalised analytically). The Bayes factor ln B(signal : noise) grows as roughly ½ SNR²; the equivalent Gaussian significance is Z ≈ √(2 ln B).

Particle physics: discovery by the numbers

The convention that a discovery needs 5σ (a chance probability below ~3×10−7) exists because a wide search has many places to fluctuate — the look-elsewhere effect — so the local significance must be large after the trials correction. On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS each reported a 125 GeV boson at 5σ; the Bayesian evidence tells the same story through the Bayes factor between “background only” and “background + Higgs.”

One engine, three sciences. Cosmology, exoplanets, and detection (from RFI to the Higgs) all run the identical calculation — marginalise the linear parameters, integrate the nonlinear ones, compare evidences.

One-line summary

best fit always improves  •  evidence peaks at the truth  •  that gap is Occam’s razor

Reproducible from evidence.py (bump counting, JAX) and poly_evidence.py (polynomial degree, closed-form NumPy). Methods covered: closed-form linear–Gaussian marginalisation, Laplace / Occam factor, BIC, nested sampling, thermodynamic integration, Savage–Dickey, and neural evidence estimators. Styling matches the planetary & space-weather demo deck.
